newsitem.title: PARAGUAY: Latam foreign ministers seek new dialogue with U.S..
newsitem.headline: Latam foreign ministers seek new dialogue with U.S..

text.p: Foreign ministers from eight Latin American nations met on Saturday to discuss unilateral U.S. actions affecting their region and suggest alternatives.

Mexico, Colombia and Venezuela will seek condemnation of unilateral moves such as the U.S. drug certification process, which punishes countries not deemed to be cooperating with Washington in the war on drug trafficking, delegates said.
Mexico, opposed to a new U.S. immigration law that could lead to the deportation of thousands of illegal immigrants, will also propose ways to end discrimination in immigration policy, they said.
The 14-nation Group of Rio, which last year rejected the Helms-Burton law tightening the U.S. embargo on Cuba, wants the U.S. government to adopt a more multilateral approach.

"Mexico, Venezuela and Colombia will propose a total rejection of unilateral actions on economic, social and antidrug policy matters," Colombian minister Maria Emma Mejia told reporters before the start of the two-day meeting.

On anti-drug policy, she said Colombia would try to get its Latin partners to strengthen multilateral action through the Organization of American States, which has a Center for Anti-Drug Intelligence Coordination.
The United States last year "decertified" Colombia for the second consecutive year as a trustworthy ally in the drug war. Mexico was certified despite opposition by the U.S. Congress.
The Rio Group issued a statement in March rejecting the U.S. certification process as an unfair unilateral action.

Paraguayan Foreign Minister Ruben Melgarejo said Latin nations hope to establish a new dialogue with the United States at the second presidential Summit of the Americas, to be held in Santiago, Chile, next March.
The Rio Group is an informal forum for consultations between South American countries, Mexico, Panama and one representative each from Central America and the Caribbean.
Only Bolivia, Colombia, Mexico, Panama, Chile, Peru and Venezuela sent their foreign ministers to the Paraguay meeting.
